questions.q: Which definition is printed for the inflammatory muscle diseases?
opts: A motor-neuron disease with fasciculations and wasting
A multisystem autoimmune connective-tissue disease with mononuclear inflammation within skeletal muscle and subacute weakness, lasting 6-8 weeks
A monophasic post-viral myalgia of the calves lasting days
A dystrophic muscle disease with dystrophin loss
questions.exp: Definition: a multisystem autoimmune CTD characterised by mononuclear inflammation within skeletal muscle, with subacute muscle weakness and fatigue, lasting 6-8 weeks. (Book p477)

questions.q: Which entities are listed in the OLD classification of the inflammatory muscle diseases?
opts: Only dermatomyositis and polymyositis
Only inclusion body myositis
Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
Dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome and juvenile dermatomyositis
questions.exp: Old classification: polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy. (Book p477)

questions.q: Which term does the CURRENT classification declare obsolete?
opts: Dermatomyositis
Inclusion body myositis
Antisynthetase syndrome
Polymyositis
questions.exp: Current classification opens with polymyositis, now an obsolete term, and then lists dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome, necrotizing myopathies, juvenile DM, paraneoplastic myositis, inclusion body myositis and amyopathic DM. (Book p477)

questions.q: A patient reports progressive difficulty rising from a chair and lifting the head off the pillow over two months, with new dysphagia. Which Bohan-Peter criterion does this satisfy?
opts: Proximal and symmetrical weakness of the pelvic and scapular girdle and anterior neck flexors progressing over weeks to months, with or without dysphagia or respiratory-muscle involvement
Elevation of serum skeletal-muscle enzymes
Electromyography characteristic of myopathy
Muscle biopsy showing necrosis and inflammatory exudate
questions.exp: Criterion A: proximal and symmetrical muscle weakness of the pelvic and scapular girdle and anterior flexors of the neck, progressing for weeks to months, with or without dysphagia or involvement of respiratory muscles. (Book p477)

questions.q: Blood tests in a patient with suspected myositis show a raised creatine kinase with raised AST, LDH and aldolase. Which Bohan-Peter criterion does this satisfy?
opts: Amylase and lipase
Creatine kinase, aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase and aldolase
Troponin, CK-MB and myoglobin only
Alanine aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase only
questions.exp: Criterion B: elevation of serum levels of skeletal-muscle enzymes, namely creatine kinase, aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase and aldolase. (Book p477)

questions.q: Electromyography in a weak patient shows short small motor units with fibrillation, positive sharp waves and insertional irritability. Which criterion does this satisfy?
opts: Myasthenic decremental response on repetitive stimulation
A purely neuropathic pattern with fibrillation only
Short small motor units with fibrillation, positive sharp waves, insertional irritability and repetitive high-frequency firing
Long large motor units with a reduced recruitment pattern only
questions.exp: Criterion C: EMG characteristic of myopathy with short and small motor units, fibrillation, positive sharp waves, insertional irritability and repetitive high-frequency firing. (Book p477)

questions.q: What is printed under Bohan-Peter criterion D?
opts: A normal muscle biopsy with no inflammation
Perifascicular atrophy with complement deposition
Red-rimmed vacuoles
Muscle biopsy showing necrosis, phagocytosis and inflammatory exudate
questions.exp: Criterion D: muscle biopsy showing necrosis, phagocytosis and inflammatory exudate. (Book p477)

questions.q: A weak patient has a violaceous periorbital rash with periorbital oedema and vasculitic lesions over the MCP joints. Which Bohan-Peter item does this fulfil?
opts: Heliotrope rash with periorbital oedema and violaceous erythema, and Gottron's sign over the elbows, MCP and PIP joints
Gottron papules and mechanic's hands
Malar rash and discoid plaques
Lupus pernio and erythema nodosum
questions.exp: Typical cutaneous changes: heliotrope rash with periorbital oedema and violaceous erythema, and Gottron's sign with vasculitis in the elbow, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. (Book p477)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which genetic risk factors are printed for dermatomyositis?
opts: HLA-A29 and HLA-B44
HLA-DRB1*03 and HLA-DRB1*07
HLA-B27 and HLA-B51
HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8
questions.exp: Risk factors, genetic: HLA-DRB1-03 and HLA-DRB1-07. (Book p477)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: A patient taking a statin and chloroquine for many years develops dermatomyositis. Which environmental exposures does the source list?
opts: Ionising radiation and benzene only
No environmental factors are listed
UV B rays, Coxsackie and parvovirus B19 infection, and the drugs chloroquine, colchicine and statins
Smoking and silica only
questions.exp: Environmental risk factors: UV B rays, Coxsackie and parvovirus B19 virus, and drugs including chloroquine, colchicine and statins. (Book p477)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which HLA-disease pairings are printed in the note on HLA risk factors?
opts: DR3 with scleroderma; DR4 with SLE; DR5 with Sjogren syndrome
DR2 with myasthenia; DR3 with vasculitis
HLA associations are not printed for myositis
DR3 with SLE, Sjogren syndrome and dermatomyositis; DR4 with APS and RA; DR5 with scleroderma
questions.exp: The note lists 03 with SLE, Sjogren's and dermatomyositis, 04 with APS and RA, and 05 with scleroderma. (Book p478)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which demographic pattern is printed for the typical presentation of PM/DM?
opts: Most commonly middle-aged, adult onset 40-60 years (juvenile 5-15 years), with females outnumbering males 2:1
Most commonly in the elderly over 80, with male predominance
Exclusively in children under 5 years
Equal sex distribution at all ages
questions.exp: Typical (55-60%): most commonly middle-aged; juvenile 5-15 years, adult 40-60 years, females more than males (2:1). (Book p478)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: A 45-year-old woman reports two months of symmetrical proximal weakness without pain or sensory loss. Which features does the source describe as typical?
opts: Fatigable weakness worsening with repetition
Bilateral, symmetrical, purely motor and proximal, with no significant pain and progression over weeks to months
Unilateral, distal and painful with sensory loss
Ascending areflexic paralysis with sensory involvement
questions.exp: Typical features: weakness that is bilateral and symmetrical, purely motor, proximal, autoimmune (acquired), persistent, with no significant pain and progressive motor weakness over weeks to months. (Book p478)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which examination findings are printed for the muscular presentation?
opts: Normal power with fasciculations and absent reflexes
Reduced power with a sensory level
Normal bulk with reduced power and tone, normal reflexes and an intact sensory system
Reduced bulk with brisk reflexes and sensory loss
questions.exp: Examination findings: bulk normal, power reduced, tone reduced, reflexes normal and sensory system intact. (Book p478)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which muscle groups are specifically spared in the inflammatory muscle diseases?
opts: Quadriceps and hip flexors
Neck flexors and respiratory muscles
Shoulder abductors
Extraocular and facial muscles
questions.exp: The note lists the muscle groups not involved in IMD as the extraocular muscles and the facial muscles. (Book p478)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which frequencies are printed for the atypical presentations of PM/DM?
opts: 30% have acute-subacute proximal pain and weakness; 10% have chronic proximal plus distal weakness
10% have acute-subacute proximal pain and weakness; 30% have chronic proximal plus distal weakness
50% have isolated distal weakness
5% have any atypical presentation
questions.exp: Atypical: 30% present with proximal pain and weakness with an acute-subacute onset, and 10% with chronic proximal plus distal weakness; the syndrome table gives the same 30 and 10 figures for the corresponding rows. (Book p478)

questions.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
questions.q: Which clinical syndrome in the frequency table runs over years rather than months?
opts: Proximal myalgia alone
Insidious proximal and distal weakness over 1-10 years
Painless proximal weakness over 3-10 months
Acute or subacute proximal pain and weakness over weeks to months
questions.exp: The syndrome table lists insidious proximal and distal weakness over 1-10 years, contrasted with painless proximal weakness over 3-10 months and acute or subacute proximal pain and weakness over weeks to months. (Book p478)

questions.q: A patient with proximal weakness has violaceous flat-topped papules over the knuckles and a periorbital violaceous rash. Which lesions does the source call pathognomonic?
opts: Shawl sign and V sign
Holster sign and periungual telangiectasia
Gottron's papules and the heliotrope rash
Mechanic's hands and Raynaud phenomenon
questions.exp: Pathognomonic skin lesions: Gottron's papule (scaly erythematous flat-topped violaceous papule/plaque over the dorsal MCP, PIP and DIP) and heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema). (Book p479)

questions.q: How is Gottron's papule described?
opts: A tender subcutaneous nodule over the shins
A purpuric macule on the buttocks
A keratotic plug on the palms only
A scaly, erythematous, flat-topped violaceous papule or plaque over the dorsal surface of MCP, PIP and DIP joints
questions.exp: Gottron's papule: scaly erythematous flat-topped violaceous papule/plaque on the dorsal surface of MCP, PIP and DIP joints. (Book p479)

questions.q: A patient with myositis has violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema. What is this rash called?
opts: Violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema
A violaceous plaque over the knuckles
A photosensitive rash over the upper back
A periungual erythematous telangiectasia
questions.exp: Heliotrope rash: violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema. (Book p479)

questions.q: How does the source distinguish Gottron's sign from Gottron's papule?
opts: There is no difference between the two
Gottron's sign is the macular erythema over the papule, typically on extensor surfaces and photosensitive, with linear erythema over the dorsum of the hand
Gottron's sign is the same lesion on the elbow only
Gottron's sign is a scarring variant
questions.exp: Other skin lesions: Gottron rash/sign is macular erythema over Gottron's papule, typically on extensor surfaces, photosensitive, with linear erythema over the dorsum of the hand. (Book p479)

questions.q: A patient has a photosensitive erythematous rash over the chest and upper back, with a further patch on the lateral thigh. Which signs does the source name?
opts: All three are on the face
All three are on the lower legs
V sign over the chest; shawl sign posteriorly over the back; holster sign on the lateral aspect of the thigh
V sign over the back; shawl sign over the chest; holster sign on the arm
questions.exp: V sign is located over the chest, shawl sign posteriorly over the back and holster sign is erythema on the lateral aspect of the thigh; scalp involvement is generally pruritic. (Book p479)

questions.q: Which nail-fold findings are listed under telangiectasia?
opts: Splinter haemorrhages with nail pitting
Onycholysis with subungual hyperkeratosis
Beau's lines with nail loss
Periungual erythema or oedema with cuticular hyperplasia
questions.exp: Telangiectasia: nail-fold capillary involvement with periungual erythema or oedema, and cuticular hyperplasia also seen. (Book p479)

questions.q: A child with dermatomyositis develops firm subcutaneous deposits over the extremities. Which statements does the source make about calcinosis cutis?
opts: It is due to deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite, is seen in juvenile dermatomyositis and also occurs in CREST syndrome
It is due to urate deposition and occurs only in gout
It is due to amorphous calcium phosphate and occurs only in SLE
It is a feature of adult dermatomyositis alone
questions.exp: Calcinosis cutis: also seen in CREST syndrome and in juvenile dermatomyositis, and due to deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite. (Book p479)

questions.q: How does the dermatomyositis rash differ from the SLE rash on this page?
opts: The DM rash is always associated with oral ulcers
The DM rash involves the knuckles, spares the nasolabial fold, is pruritic and is not associated with oral ulcers
The DM rash spares the knuckles and involves the nasolabial fold
The two rashes are indistinguishable
questions.exp: SLE rash: never involves the knuckles, may involve the nasolabial fold, associated with painless oral cavity ulcers and non-pruritic. Dermatomyositis rash: involves the knuckles (MCP joint), does not involve the nasolabial fold, not associated with oral cavity ulcers and pruritic. (Book p480)

questions.q: Which statement about mechanic's hand is printed?
opts: It is diagnostic of systemic sclerosis
It indicates underlying malignancy
It is not specific for dermatomyositis and forms part of the antisynthetase syndrome
It is pathognomonic of dermatomyositis
questions.exp: Mechanic's hand: not specific for dermatomyositis and part of the antisynthetase syndrome. (Book p480)

questions.q: A definitive test is needed in a patient with suspected inflammatory muscle disease. Which investigation does the source call the gold standard?
opts: Serum creatine kinase
Electromyography
Whole-body MRI
Muscle biopsy
questions.exp: Muscle biopsy is described as the gold standard test. (Book p480)

questions.q: Which muscle-biopsy features are printed for dermatomyositis?
opts: Mononuclear (CD4-positive T-cell) infiltrate with perifascicular atrophy
CD8-positive T-cell endomysial invasion without atrophy
Red-rimmed vacuoles with amyloid deposits
Necrotizing fibres with no inflammation
questions.exp: Muscle biopsy shows a mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate of CD4+ T cells and perifascicular atrophy. (Book p480)

questions.q: Which MRI sequence and finding are printed?
opts: Diffusion-weighted imaging showing restricted diffusion
STIR sequence showing hyperintense areas
T1 sequence showing hypointense fibrosis only
Gradient echo showing haemosiderin
questions.exp: MRI: the STIR sequence shows hyperintense areas within muscle. (Book p480)

questions.q: Which electromyographic findings are listed in the investigations block?
opts: A decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation
Prolonged insertion with myotonic discharges only
Polyphasic short-duration small-amplitude potentials with high-frequency discharges and spontaneous fibrillation
Large polyphasic units with a reduced interference pattern
questions.exp: EMG: polyphasic short-duration small-amplitude potentials, high-frequency discharges, and spontaneous fibrillation or denervation. (Book p480)

questions.q: Enzymes in a patient with myositis show a creatine kinase above the AST. Which enzyme relationship does the source print?
opts: AST exceeds CPK
Aldolase is the dominant enzyme
LDH is the only useful enzyme
CPK exceeds AST
questions.exp: Enzymes: CPK is greater than AST. (Book p480)

questions.q: Which antibody and prognostic profile is printed on this page?
opts: Anti-Mi-2 alpha: good prognosis, low risk for ILD and responsive to conventional therapy with steroid and MMF
Anti-Jo-1: good prognosis with no ILD risk
Anti-SRP: excellent steroid response
Anti-MDA-5: low risk of rapidly progressive ILD
questions.exp: Antibody associated: anti-Mi-2 alpha with good prognosis, low risk for ILD and responsiveness to conventional therapy (steroid plus MMF). (Book p480)

questions.q: How do the age groups differ between polymyositis and dermatomyositis in the comparison table?
opts: Both occur only in children
Polymyositis occurs only in adults; dermatomyositis is also seen in the elderly and in juveniles
Dermatomyositis occurs only in adults; polymyositis also occurs in children
Both are confined to middle-aged adults
questions.exp: Age group: polymyositis only in adults; dermatomyositis seen in the elderly or juvenile. (Book p481)

questions.q: A patient with biopsy-proven myositis has no skin rash and no calcinosis. Which rows of the source's comparison table best separate the two entities?
opts: Serum enzymes: raised in polymyositis, normal in dermatomyositis
EMG: abnormal in polymyositis, normal in dermatomyositis
Skin changes and calcinosis: absent or rare in polymyositis, present in dermatomyositis
Weakness distribution: distal in polymyositis, proximal in dermatomyositis
questions.exp: Skin changes are absent in polymyositis and present in dermatomyositis; calcinosis is rare in polymyositis and seen in dermatomyositis. Both share subacute onset, proximal symmetric weakness, systemic features and normal-to-high enzymes. (Book p481)

questions.q: Which overlap statement is printed for the two entities?
opts: Dermatomyositis never exists on its own
Neither is associated with overlap syndromes
Both always occur as isolated diseases
Polymyositis never exists on its own, whereas dermatomyositis can exist on its own
questions.exp: Associated systemic conditions or overlap syndrome: yes for polymyositis, which never exists on its own, and yes for dermatomyositis, which can exist on its own. (Book p481)

questions.q: Which biopsy immunology distinguishes the two conditions?
opts: Polymyositis shows CD8-positive T-cell involvement; dermatomyositis shows CD4-positive and B-cell involvement with perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation
Both show identical CD8-positive endomysial infiltrates
Both show red-rimmed vacuoles
Neither shows any inflammatory infiltrate
questions.exp: Biopsy findings: polymyositis shows CD8+ T-cell involvement while dermatomyositis shows CD4+ and B cells with perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation. (Book p481)

questions.q: Which prognostic statement opens the antisynthetase syndrome block?
opts: It requires no treatment
It is treatable if diagnosed early
It is uniformly fatal within a year
It never responds to immunosuppression
questions.exp: The antisynthetase syndrome block opens with the statement that it is treatable if diagnosed early. (Book p481)

questions.q: A patient with myositis has roughened skin on the radial side of the index finger, Raynaud phenomenon, cardiomyopathy and an SLE-like arthritis. Which syndrome and features does the source list?
opts: Proximal myalgia with a normal CK
Isolated ILD with no systemic features
Mechanic's hand, Raynaud phenomenon, cardiomyopathy and an SLE-like arthritis (Jaccoud arthropathy)
Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules and calcinosis
questions.exp: Antisynthetase syndrome clinical features: mechanic's hand, Raynaud's phenomenon, cardiomyopathy and an SLE-like arthritis (Jaccoud's arthropathy). (Book p481)

questions.q: How does the source describe mechanic's hand in the antisynthetase syndrome?
opts: Violaceous papules over the dorsal MCP joints
Periungual telangiectasia with cuticular overgrowth
Painless nodules over the Achilles tendon
Crusted hyperkeratotic lesions on the radial aspect of the index and middle fingers
questions.exp: Mechanic's hand is seen on the radial aspect of the index and middle finger and is characterised by crusted hyperkeratotic lesions. (Book p481)

questions.q: Which additional disease association is printed for Jaccoud's arthropathy?
opts: It is also seen in Sjogren syndrome
It is also seen in sarcoidosis
It is pathognomonic of rheumatoid arthritis
It occurs only in the antisynthetase syndrome
questions.exp: The note adds that Jaccoud's arthropathy is also seen in Sjogren's syndrome. (Book p481)

questions.q: A patient with the antisynthetase syndrome has fever and pulmonary infiltrates on the chest radiograph. What does the source warn about?
opts: It is a benign self-limiting finding
It can be mistaken for viral pneumonia and can progress to ILD, which is the most common cause of death
It is always a bacterial pneumonia needing antibiotics
It indicates an acute coronary syndrome
questions.exp: Investigations: CXR shows fever with infiltrates, which can be mistaken for viral pneumonia and can progress into ILD; ILD can be the first presentation of the syndrome and is the most common cause of death. (Book p481)

questions.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
questions.q: HRCT in a patient with myositis shows ground-glass opacities with areas of consolidation. Which interstitial patterns does the source print?
opts: Only cryptogenic organising pneumonia
Only usual interstitial pneumonia
NSIP and COP, with NSIP most common and identified by ground-glass opacities
UIP and LIP, with UIP most common
questions.exp: ILD pattern: NSIP plus COP. NSIP is most common and identified by ground-glass opacities; COP is identified by consolidations. (Book p482)

questions.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
questions.q: Which imaging signature is attached to a UIP pattern in these patients?
opts: Ground-glass opacities without destruction
Consolidation with air bronchograms
Cavitation with an air-fluid level
Honeycombing with destruction of the lung parenchyma
questions.exp: The note states UIP in the lung is identified by a honeycombing structure, that is destruction of the parenchyma. (Book p482)

questions.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
questions.q: Which antibody and prognosis are attached to amyopathic dermatomyositis?
opts: Anti-MDA-5 with a poor prognosis that is not treatable
Anti-Mi-2 with an excellent prognosis
Anti-Jo-1 with a good treatment response
Anti-SRP with reversible disease
questions.exp: Amyopathic DM: poor prognosis and not treatable, with anti-MDA-5 antibody and a clinical triad featuring rapidly progressive ILD. (Book p482)

questions.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
questions.q: An 8-year-old girl with dermatomyositis has no cardiac involvement, no malignancy and no interstitial lung disease. Which pattern does the source print for juvenile disease?
opts: Boys are affected twice as often as girls
Malignancy, cardiac involvement and ILD are absent; girls aged 5-15 years are commonly affected
Malignancy is common in juvenile disease
Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death
questions.exp: Juvenile DM commonly affects girls aged 5-15 years and malignancy, cardiac involvement and ILD are absent. (Book p482)

questions.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
questions.q: Which antibodies are printed for juvenile dermatomyositis, and what does their presence in an adult imply?
opts: Anti-SRP and anti-HMG-CoA reductase; in adults they indicate statin exposure
Anti-MDA-5 alone; in adults they indicate rapidly progressive ILD
Anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1-gamma; in adults they indicate cancer-associated myositis
Anti-Jo-1 and anti-Mi-2; in adults they indicate overlap disease
questions.exp: Juvenile DM antibodies are anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1-gamma; if seen in adults they indicate cancer-associated myositis. (Book p482)

questions.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
questions.q: Which antibody and treatment-response pairings are printed for immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy?
opts: Both antibodies respond fully to steroids alone
Anti-SRP responds rapidly and anti-HMG-CoA reductase does not
Neither antibody is associated with treatment response
Anti-SRP in severe disease with ILD and cardiac involvement does not respond; anti-HMG-CoA reductase after statin therapy responds to steroid, IVIG and rituximab
questions.exp: Immune-mediated necrotizing DM: anti-SRP in severe disease with ILD and cardiac manifestations does not respond; anti-HMG-CoA reductase, seen with statin therapy, responds to steroid plus IVIG plus rituximab (rarely). (Book p482)

questions.q: An elderly man presents with recurrent falls and slowly progressive weakness. Which demographic and presenting pattern does the source print?
opts: Most common in the elderly with male predominance, presenting with recurrent falls and a chronic course
Most common in young women with an acute febrile onset
Most common in children with a rash
Most common in middle-aged women with proximal weakness only
questions.exp: IBM: most common in the elderly (males more than females), presenting with recurrent falls and a chronic presentation. (Book p483)

questions.q: How is the weakness of inclusion body myositis described?
opts: Facial and ocular weakness
Asymmetrical proximal and distal involvement, including quadriceps, vastus and finger flexors
Symmetrical proximal weakness only
Purely distal sensory loss
questions.exp: IBM weakness is asymmetrical, proximal plus distal, and involves the quadriceps, vastus and finger flexors. (Book p483)

questions.q: A muscle biopsy shows red-rimmed vacuoles and the patient has not improved on steroids. Which histology and treatment response does the source print?
opts: Necrotizing fibres responding to rituximab
Non-caseating granulomas responding to methotrexate
Red-rimmed vacuoles with a steroid-unresponsive course
Perifascicular atrophy with an excellent steroid response
questions.exp: IBM histology shows red-rimmed vacuoles and the disease is steroid unresponsive. (Book p483)

questions.q: Which malignancies are paired with dermatomyositis on this page?
opts: Breast cancer is characteristic and colon cancer the most common
Gastric cancer is characteristic and lymphoma the most common
Prostate cancer is characteristic and melanoma the most common
Ovarian cancer is characteristic and lung cancer is the most common
questions.exp: Cancers associated with DM: carcinoma ovary is characteristic and carcinoma lung is the most common. (Book p483)

questions.q: Which antibody is printed for the antisynthetase syndrome in the antibody table?
opts: Anti-Jo-1
Anti-Mi-2 alpha
Anti-MDA-5
Anti-Ku
questions.exp: Antibodies specific to IMDs: dermatomyositis with anti-Mi-2 alpha, antisynthetase syndrome with anti-Jo-1, necrotizing myopathy with anti-SRP and anti-HMG-CoA reductase, amyopathic DM with anti-MDA-5, and juvenile DM and cancer-associated myositis with anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1-gamma. (Book p483)

questions.q: Which antibodies are listed as OTHER associated antibodies, and what is noted for two of them?
opts: Anti-RNA polymerase III and anti-U1 RNP
Anti-Ro, anti-Ku (which may develop ILD) and anti-PM/Scl (polymyositis with scleroderma with or without ILD and a nucleolar ANA pattern)
Anti-centromere and anti-topoisomerase
Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm
questions.exp: Other associated antibodies: anti-Ro; anti-Ku, which may develop ILD; and anti-PM/Scl, seen in polymyositis with scleroderma with or without ILD and showing an ANA nucleolar pattern. (Book p483)

questions.q: Which antibodies are shared by juvenile dermatomyositis and cancer-associated myositis?
opts: Anti-Mi-2 and anti-MDA-5
Anti-Ku and anti-Ro
Anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1-gamma
Anti-Jo-1 and anti-SRP
questions.exp: Both juvenile DM and cancer-associated myositis are listed with anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1-gamma. (Book p483)

questions.q: What is the printed first-line treatment for the inflammatory muscle diseases?
opts: Steroid alone in pulsed doses only
Methotrexate monotherapy
Intravenous immunoglobulin alone
Steroid plus methotrexate, or steroid plus mycophenolate mofetil
questions.exp: Treatment: the goal is clinical elimination of all disease activity; first line is steroid plus MTX or steroid plus MMF. (Book p483)

questions.q: Which agents are listed as second-line treatment?
opts: Rituximab and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib
Cyclophosphamide and azathioprine
Anti-TNF agents and anakinra
Plasma exchange alone
questions.exp: Second-line treatment: rituximab and JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib). (Book p483)

questions.q: What is stated as the goal of treatment for the inflammatory muscle diseases?
opts: Lifelong steroid monotherapy
Clinical elimination of all disease activity
Normalisation of the muscle biopsy
Normalisation of the EMG
questions.exp: The treatment goal is clinical elimination of all disease activity. (Book p483)

units.title: 1. Definition, Classification & Bohan-Peter Criteria
units.guide:
The definition sets the time course and the inflammatory target before any classification.
Old and current classifications are contrasted, with polymyositis now an obsolete term.
The Bohan-Peter criteria then list the clinical, enzymatic, electrophysiological, biopsy and cutaneous items.

units.title: 2. Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
units.sec: Risk Factors, HLA Links & Muscular Presentation
units.guide:
Risk factors are split into genetic and environmental, with drugs among the environmental triggers.
The HLA note then places dermatomyositis among the other HLA-associated connective-tissue diseases.
The typical muscular presentation and the syndrome-frequency table follow.

units.title: 3. Skin Manifestations
units.guide:
Pathognomonic lesions are separated from the wider set of skin signs.
Each lesion is then localised to its characteristic site.
Calcinosis cutis closes the list with its chemistry and its associations.

units.title: 4. Rash Comparison & Investigations
units.guide:
A comparison note separates the dermatomyositis rash from the SLE rash.
Investigations then run from biopsy through MRI and EMG to enzymes and antibody prognostication.
Mechanic's hand is placed in the antisynthetase group rather than being disease specific.

units.title: 5. Polymyositis vs Dermatomyositis & Antisynthetase Syndrome
units.guide:
The comparison table contrasts the two classic entities feature by feature.
Biopsy immunology is the discriminator when the clinical features overlap.
The antisynthetase syndrome is then presented as a treatable early-diagnosis entity.

units.title: 6. ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
units.sec: ILD Patterns, Amyopathic & Juvenile DM, Necrotizing Myopathy
units.guide:
The ILD patterns of the myositides are named with their imaging signatures.
Amyopathic and juvenile dermatomyositis are then contrasted by prognosis and antibodies.
The necrotizing myopathy table maps antibody to cause and treatment response.

units.title: 7. Inclusion Body Myositis, Antibodies & Treatment
units.guide:
Inclusion body myositis is set apart by its distribution, histology and steroid resistance.
Antibody tables then map each myositis subset and its malignancy links.
The treatment ladder closes the chapter with first- and second-line choices.
